nodes.name: Van der Waerden's theorem
nodes.statement: Van der Waerden~\cite{VDW} showed that in any finite coloring of the integers, there are arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions.
assumptions: any finite coloring of the integers
conclusions: there are arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions

nodes.statement_short: Any finite coloring of N admits an infinite B whose pairwise sums of distinct elements are monochromatic.

nodes.statement: For example, amongst them was the statement that every positive density set of natural numbers contains the sum \[ B+C := \{ b+c:b\in B,~ c\in C \} \] of two infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: every positive density set of natural numbers
conclusions: contains the sum

nodes.name: Positive integers and multiples
nodes.statement: Throughout we let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ denote the positive integers and for $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $k\mathbb{N}=\{kn:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ denote the set of all positive multiples of $k$.

nodes.name: Upper Banach density
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a set of natural numbers, define its \define{upper Banach density} $\mathsf{d}^*(A)$ to be \begin{equation} \mathsf{d}^*(A):=\limsup_{N -M\to \infty} \frac{\big|A\cap \{M+1,M+2,\dots,N\}\big|}{N-M}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Upper Banach density d*(A): limsup of the proportion of A in intervals of growing length.

nodes.name: Upper Banach density formula
nodes.statement: \mathsf{d}^*(A):=\limsup_{N -M\to \infty} \frac{\big|A\cap \{M+1,M+2,\dots,N\}\big|}{N-M}.
nodes.label: eqn:positive_upper_density

nodes.name: Upper and lower density
nodes.statement: The \define{upper density} $\overline{\mathsf{d}}(A)$ and \define{lower density} $\underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)$ of $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ are defined respectively as \[ \overline{\mathsf{d}}(A)=\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N} \quad\text{and}\quad \underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N}. \]

nodes.name: Natural density
nodes.statement: If $\overline{\mathsf{d}}(A) = \underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)$, then we call this number the \define{natural density} of $A$ and denote it by $\mathsf{d}(A)$.

nodes.name: Følner sequence in N
nodes.statement: In some settings, we use density with respect to a \define{F\o{}lner{} sequence} in $\mathbb{N}$, meaning a sequence $\Phi=(\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ satisfying $$ \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{|(\Phi_N+t)\cap \Phi_N|}{| \Phi_N|} = 1 $$ for all $t\in\mathbb{N}$, where $\Phi_N+t$ denotes the shift of the set $\Phi_N$ by $t$.
nodes.statement_short: A Følner sequence is a sequence of finite sets nearly invariant under every shift.

nodes.name: Upper and lower density along a Følner sequence
nodes.statement: Analogous to upper and lower density, the \define{upper} and \define{lower density along $\Phi$} of a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ are defined as \[ \overline{\mathsf{d}}_\Phi(A) = \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} \quad \text{and} \quad \underline{\mathsf{d}}_\Phi(A)=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|}. \]

nodes.name: Density along a Følner sequence
nodes.statement: When the quantities above are equal, we denote the common value by $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)$ and call it the \define{density} of $A$ along $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Finite sums set
nodes.statement: Given a set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$, its \define{finite sums set} is defined by \begin{equation} \mathsf{FS}(B) = \left\{ \sum_{n \in F} n : F \subset B\textup{ with } 0< |F| < \infty \right\} \end{equation} and consists of all natural numbers obtained by adding together finitely many distinct elements in $B$.

nodes.statement_short: FS(B) is the set of all sums of finitely many distinct elements of B.

nodes.name: Finite sums set FS(B)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{FS}(B) = \left\{ \sum_{n \in F} n : F \subset B\textup{ with } 0< |F| < \infty \right\}

nodes.name: IP-set
nodes.statement: When $B$ is infinite we say that $\mathsf{FS}(B)$ is an \emph{IP-set}\footnote{Depending on the source, the acronym IP stands for \emph{infinite parallelepiped}~\cite{FW79} or \emph{idempotent}~\cite{FK85}, where the latter relates to the Stone-{\v C}ech compactification of the integers.}.

nodes.name: Erdős's shifted IP-set question
nodes.statement: In a first attempt to formulate a density version of Hindman's theorem, Erd\H{o}s{} asked whether every set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with positive upper density has a shift\[ A-t := \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : t + n \in A \} \] for some integer $t\geq 0$ that contains an IP-set.

nodes.statement_short: Erdős asked whether every positive upper density set has a shift A-t containing an IP-set (answered negatively by Straus).

nodes.name: Straus example
nodes.statement: Let $(p_t)_{t\geq 1}$ be a sufficiently fast growing sequence of primes and let $$A:=\mathbb{N}\setminus\left(\bigcup_{t\in\mathbb{N}}(p_t\mathbb{N}+t)\right)$$ Then $\mathsf{d}(A)\geq1-\sum_{t=1}^\infty\frac1{p_t}>0$ but any shift $A-t$ of $A$ contains only finitely many multiples of $p_t$ and hence cannot contain an IP-set.

nodes.statement: Every set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of positive upper Banach density contains a sumset \[t+\big\{ b_1+b_2:b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1\neq b_2 \big\}\] for some shift $t\geq0$ and some infinite set $B \subset A$.

nodes.name: Leth's example: no B+B+t
nodes.statement: For $c\in(1,2)$ consider the set \begin{equation} A = \mathbb{N} \cap \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[4^{n},c\cdot4^{n}\right), \end{equation} which has $\mathsf{d}^*(A)=1$ and $\underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)>0$. The set $A$ does not contain any set of the form $\{b, 2b\}$ for $b \in \mathbb{N}$. When $b$ is much larger than $b'$ one cannot find $\{b+b',2b\}$ in $A$ either. One can use this observation to show that $A$ does not contain an unrestricted sumset $B+B$ for an infinite set $B$. In fact, every shift of $A$ has the same property, and so $A$ cannot contain any set of the form $B+B+t$ with $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ infinite and $t\geq 0$ integer. The proofs of these statements are deferred to the more general setting of \cref{example_nextexamplebutnowitsgone}.

nodes.statement: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item \cref{conj:bbbt}. \item For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ there exist an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and integer $t\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ with $B^{\oplus k}+t\subset A$. \item For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A\cap k\mathbb{N})>0$ there exists an infinite set $B\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $B^{\oplus k}\subset A$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Clearly the second statement implies the first. To see how the third statement implies the second, let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ and find $t\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ such that $A':=A\cap (k\mathbb{N}+t)$ has $\mathsf{d}^*(A')>0$. Then $A'-t\subset k\mathbb{N}$ and by the third statement there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $B^{\oplus k}\subset A'-t$. To show that the first statement implies the third, let $A\subset k\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ and, using the first statement, find $t\geq0$ and an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $B^{\oplus k}+t\subset A\subset k\mathbb{N}$. Now $B$ must contain $k$ elements which are all congruent modulo $k$, and therefore their sum is a multiple of $k$. It follows that $t=k\tilde{t}$ for some $\tilde{t}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Letting $\tilde{B}=B+\tilde{t}$ we conclude that $\tilde{B}^{\oplus k}\subset A$.

nodes.name: Conjecture 2.9 follows from Conjecture 2.4

nodes.name: Local obstruction to all sub-sums
nodes.statement: One may be tempted to ask whether $A$ contains all sums \[ B_{i(1)} + \cdots + B_{i(r)} \] for all $1 \le i(1) < \cdots < i(r) \le k$ for some $r$ with $2\leq r \leq k$. However, there are local obstructions to this and in particular the set $A=2\mathbb{N}-1$ does not contain such a configuration.

nodes.name: Syndetic set
nodes.statement: Subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ with bounded gaps are called \define{syndetic}. Equivalently, a set $S \subset \mathbb{N}$ is syndetic if there exists $h\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $(S-1) \cup (S-2) \cup \cdots \cup (S-h) = \mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Sumsets from syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Fix $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A) > 0$. For any syndetic subsets $P$ and $Q$ of $\mathbb{N}$ there is $P' \subset P$ infinite and $Q' \subset Q$ infinite and $t \ge 0$ with $P' + Q' + t \subset A$.
conclusions: there is $P' \subset P$ infinite and $Q' \subset Q$ infinite and $t \ge 0$ with $P' + Q' + t \subset A$
nodes.label: prop_syndeticB+C

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: By \cref{thm:MRR}, there exist infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $B+C\subset A$. Since $P$ and $Q$ are syndetic, we can find shifts $p,q\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $(P+p)\cap B$ and $(Q+q)\cap C$ are both infinite. Take \begin{align*} P' &= ((P+p)\cap B)-p=P\cap(B-p) \\ Q' &= ((Q+q)\cap C)-q=Q\cap(C-q) \end{align*} and $t=p+q$. We have that $P'+Q'\subset B+C-t\subset A-t$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2.7 and shift B, C to meet the syndetic sets P, Q.

nodes.name: Shift in Proposition 3.1 is needed

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: The implication $ \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} \Rightarrow \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} $ follows from a careful analysis of the proof in~\cite{MRR} (or the proofs in~\cite{Host} and in~\cite{KMRR}). The proof of $ \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} \Rightarrow \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} $ is by construction. If $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(W)=0$ we can find a slowly growing sequence $f\colon \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n)=\infty$ and such that the set \[ \tilde W := \bigcup_{w\in W}[w-f(w),w+f(w)] \] still has $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(\tilde W)=0$. Letting $A=\mathbb{N}\setminus\tilde W$ we see that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$. Whenever $A$ contains a sumset $B+C$ and $C\subset W$, if $b\in B$ and $w\in W$ are such that $f(w)>b$, then we cannot have $w\in C$ (as $w+b\notin A$). nodes.name: Thick and piecewise syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Recall that a set $T\subset\mathbb{N}$ is \define{thick} if it contains arbitrarily long blocks of consecutive integers. The properties of being thick and being syndetic are dual in the following sense: a set is thick if and only if it has nonempty intersection with every syndetic set, and vice versa. A set $P \subset \mathbb{N}$ is \define{piecewise syndetic} if there is a syndetic set $S \subset \mathbb{N}$ and a thick set $T \subset \mathbb{N}$ such that $P = S \cap T$.
nodes.statement_short: Thick: contains arbitrarily long intervals; piecewise syndetic: intersection of a syndetic and a thick set.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.5
nodes.statement: The implication $ \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment2} \Rightarrow \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment2} $ is obvious. The converse implication uses Ramsey's theorem. Assuming $W$ is infinite and $A$ is syndetic, find $r\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cup(A-1)\cup\cdots\cup(A-r)=\mathbb{N}$. Then color each pair $\{w_1,w_2\}$ of elements of $W$ with the color $i\in\{0,\dots,r\}$ such that $w_1+w_2+i\in A$. Using Ramsey's theorem one can extract an infinite subset $W'\subset W$ such that every pair $\{w_1,w_2\}\subset W'$ has the same color $i$. Next split $W'$ into two disjoint infinite sets $W'=C\cup B'$ and let $B=B'+i$. It follows that $C\subset W$ and $B+C\subset A$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic obstruction to B+B+t
nodes.statement: For $x\geq 0$, let $\{x\}$ denote the fractional part of $x$. Consider the set \[ A:=\Big\{m\in\mathbb{N}:\big\{\theta\log_2(m)\big\}\in U\Big\} \] for any $\theta>0$ and any set $U\subset\mathbb{T}$ for which $U$ and $U+\theta$ (calculated $\bmod\,1$) are separated by a positive distance. Taking $\theta=1/2$ and $U=\big[0,\tfrac12\log_2(c)\big)$ for some $1 < c< 2$ we recover the set in~\eqref{eq_archemedianobstructions} of \cref{eg:not2b}. We claim that $A$ does not contain $B+B+t$ for any infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and shift $t\geq 0$. Indeed, for any infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and $t\geq 0$, we can take $b'\in B$ arbitrary and then choose $b\in B$ sufficiently large so that the difference \[ \left|\log_2\left(\frac{2b+t}{b+b'+t}\right)-1\right| \] is less than the distance $d(U,U+\theta)/\theta$. Multiplying by $\theta$ and reducing modulo one, it follows that one can not have both $b+b'+t$ and $2b+t$ in $A$. Taking $U=[0,1/2-\varepsilon]$ for small $\varepsilon>0$ and $\theta=1/2$, we have that \[ \overline{\mathsf{d}}(A)=\frac23\cdot(2-4^\varepsilon) \] As $\varepsilon\to0$ we obtain an example $A$ with upper density arbitrarily close to $2/3$. On the other hand, taking $U=[0,1/2-\varepsilon]$ and setting $\theta=1/2+n$ for some large $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (this yields the same set $A$ as setting $\theta=1/2$ and $U=T^{-1}[0,1/2-\varepsilon]$ where $T\colon\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{T}$ is multiplication by $2n+1$) one can check that \[ \underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)=\frac{2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)/\theta}-1}{2^{1/\theta}-1}. \] As $\varepsilon\to0$ and $\theta\to\infty$ it follows that $\underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)$ comes arbitrarily close to $1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Sets {m : {θ log2 m} ∈ U} avoid B+B+t; densities approach 2/3 (upper) and 1/2 (lower).

nodes.statement: Fix real numbers $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > 0$. We build, using the set in \cref{example_nextexamplebutnowitsgone} as a model, a finite coloring of $\mathbb{N}$ such that for any infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and any shift $t\geq 0$, the set $$\big\{\lfloor\lambda_1b_1+\lambda_2b_2\rfloor:b_1,b_2\in B,b_1\neq b_2\big\}+t$$ is not monochromatic. We define a finite coloring $\chi$ of the integers by setting \[ \chi(n)=\lfloor\log_{\rho}(n)\rfloor\bmod 3 \] where $\rho=\sqrt{\lambda_1/\lambda_2}>1$. Fix $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ infinite and let $b_1\in B$ be arbitrary. Let $b\in B$ be sufficiently large depending on $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,t$ and $b_1$. Let $m_1=\lfloor\lambda_1b_1+\lambda_2b\rfloor+t$ and $m_2=\lfloor\lambda_1b+\lambda_2b_1\rfloor+t$. Note that $\rho^2m_1\approx m_2$ as $b\to\infty$, so \[ \rho m_1<m_2 <\rho^3m_1 \] if we choose $b$ large enough. Taking $\log_{\rho}$ on each term we conclude that \[ \log_{\rho}(m_2)\in\Big(\log_{\rho}(m_1)+1,\log_{\rho}(m_1)+3\Big) \] and after taking floors and reducing modulo 3 we get $\chi(m_1)\neq\chi(m_2)$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic density

nodes.name: Admits correlations along Φ

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.27
nodes.statement: Since $\ghkn{\boldsymbol{1}_A-\mathsf{d}_ \Phi(A)}_\un{2}{\Phi}=0$ one can show (for completeness, the proof is given in \cref{lemma_weakmixingisback} in the appendix) that the set $A$ is weakly mixing in the sense that \[ \mathsf{d}^*\Big(\Big\{n:\big|\mathsf{d}_\Phi\big((A-n)\cap C\big)-\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)\mathsf{d}_\Phi(C)\big|>\varepsilon\Big\}\Big)=0 \] for any $\varepsilon>0$ and any set $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ for which all the implicit limits exist. Now choose $b_1\in A$ such that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi\big((A-b_1)\cap A\big)>0$. (Note that with respect to $\Phi$ a full-density set of $b_1\in A$ satisfies this.) Put $C_1:=A\cap(A-b_1)$. Recursively, for each $n=2,3,\dots$ choose $b_n\in C_{n-1}$ such that \[ \mathsf{d}_\Phi\big(C_{n-1}\cap(A-b_n)\big)>0 \] and set $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap(A-b_n)$. nodes.name: Nil-Bohr set: k-step but not (k+1)-step uniform
nodes.statement: For $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, and $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small, it can be shown that the set \[ A=\Bigl\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \{n^k\alpha\}\in \bigl[\tfrac{1}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\bigr]\Bigr\} \] satisfies $\|\boldsymbol{1}_A-\varepsilon\|_{\un{k}{\Phi}}=0$ and $\|\boldsymbol{1}_A-\varepsilon\|_{\un{k+1}{\Phi}}>0$ for all F\o{}lner{}-sequences $\Phi$ (this follows from results in~\cite{FLW-2006}). There is an infinite set $B$ such that $B\cup \cdots\cup B^{\oplus k}\subset A$ but there exists no infinite set $B$ with $B\cup \cdots\cup B^{\oplus k+1}\subset A$. We prove this claim for the case $k=2$ and leave the general case to the interested reader. The fact that \[ A=\Bigl\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \{n^2\alpha\}\in \bigl[\tfrac{1}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\bigr]\Bigr\} \] contains $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}$ follows from \cref{prop_U2_implies_no_shift_needed}. In fact, since at each stage of the inductive construction in the proof of \cref{prop_U2_implies_no_shift_needed} there is a positive density set from which the members of $B$ can be drawn, there are in a sense many sets $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ for which $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\subset A$. We are left with showing that $A$ does not contain $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\cup B^{\oplus 3}$. Let $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ be infinite. In view of Ramsey's theorem, replacing $B$ by an infinite subset of itself if needed, we can assume that for every distinct $b,b'\in B$, $\{bb'\alpha\}\approx_\varepsilon \gamma$ for some fixed $\gamma\in[0,1)$, where by $x \approx_\varepsilon y$ we mean that $|x-y| < C\varepsilon$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$. By further refining $B$ we can assume that $\{b^2\alpha\} \approx_\varepsilon \beta$ for every $b\in B$ and some $\beta\in[0,1)$. If $B\subset A$ it follows that $\beta\approx_\varepsilon1/2$. If $B\oplus B\subset A$, expanding the square $(b+b')^2\alpha$ it follows that $2(\beta+\gamma)\approx_\varepsilon1/2$. If $B^{\oplus3}\subset A$, then expanding the square $(b_1+b_2+b_3)^2\alpha$ it follows that $3\beta+6\gamma\approx_\varepsilon1/2$. Since it is impossible that $\beta$, $2\beta+2\gamma$, and $3\beta+6\gamma$ are simultaneously close to $1/2$ modulo~$1$, it follows that $A$ cannot contain $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\cup B^{\oplus 3}$.

nodes.name: Density Ramsey property
nodes.statement: We say that a collection $\mathcal{D} \subset\{F\subset\mathbb{N}\colon 0 < |F|< \infty\}$ of finite sets has the \define{density Ramsey property} if for any set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)> 0$, there exists some $X\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $X\subset A$.

nodes.name: Finitary form of the density Ramsey property
nodes.statement: By a compactness argument, the set $\mathcal{D}$ has the density Ramsey property if for all $\delta > 0$, there exists $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for any interval $J\subset\mathbb{N}$ of length at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)$ and any set $E\subset J$ with $|E|\geq \delta |J|$, there is $X\in\mathcal{D}$ with $X\subset E$.
nodes.statement_short: By compactness, the density Ramsey property holds if every δ-dense subset of a long enough interval contains a member of D.
conclusions: has the density Ramsey property

nodes.name: Szemerédi's theorem as density Ramsey property
nodes.statement: In this language, Szemer\'{e}di{}'s theorem is equivalent to the assertion that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of all $k$-term arithmetic progressions has the density Ramsey property.

nodes.name: Sumsets of sets with the density Ramsey property

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.30
nodes.statement: Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)> 0$. By combining the results in~\cite[Section~2]{MRR}, we can find $\varepsilon > 0$, a F\o lner sequence $\Phi = (\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$, and a set $L\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that for every nonempty finite set $F\subset L$, the set $$ \bigcap_{x\in F}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr)> \varepsilon\Big\} $$ has positive density with respect to $\Phi$. Let $F_1\subset F_2\subset \cdots\subset L$ be an exhaustion of $L$ by finite sets. For $i\in\mathbb{N}$, define \begin{equation} Q_i = \bigcap_{x\in F_i}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon\Big\}. \end{equation} Pick $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for any interval $J\subset\mathbb{N}$ of length at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)$ and any set $E\subset J$ with $|E|\geq \delta |J|$, there exists $X\in\mathcal{D}$ with $X\subset E$. Set $\delta_i = \mathsf{d}_\Phi(Q_i)/2$ and for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, let $J_i\subset \mathbb{N}$ denote an interval whose length is at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$ and satisfies $$|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|. $$ Without loss of generality, we can further assume that for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\max J_i < \min J_{i+1}$. Then by~\eqref{eq:def-Qi}, it follows that \begin{enumerate} \item $F_i+(Q_i\cap J_i)\subset A$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$. \item If $n_1< n_2< \cdots$ is an enumeration of $\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}(J_i\cap Q_i)$, then $$\mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon.$$ \end{enumerate} Applying Bergelson's Intersectivity Lemma~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{bergelson}, there exists $K\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ such that for all nonempty finite sets $H\subset K$, we have \begin{equation} \mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{k\in H}\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0. \end{equation} Define \[ R_i = \{n_k\colon k\in K\}\cap J_i\cap Q_i \] and let $I\subset\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set such that for all $i\in I$, we have \[ |R_i|\geq \frac{\varepsilon\delta_i}{2}|J_i| \] which exists because $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ and $|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|$. Since the length of $J_i$ exceeds $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$, we can find $X_i\in \mathcal{D}$ with $X_i\subset R_i$. Then by property~\ref{item:one} and~\eqref{eq:berg-cor}, we conclude that \begin{enumerate}[resume] \item $F_i+X_i\subset A$ for all $i\in I$. \item For each $i\in I$, we have $$\mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{x\in X_1\cup\ldots\cup X_i}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0. $$ \end{enumerate} We are now ready to inductively construct the sets $B_1, B_2,\ldots$ and $C_1, C_2, \ldots$. First choose $B_1\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $B_1\subset L$. Choose $i_1\in I$ sufficiently large such that $B_1\subset F_{i_1}$, and define $C_1 = X_{i_1}$. By Property~\eqref{item:three}, we have that $$B_1+C_1\subset A.$$ Assume we have defined the sets $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ and $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ such that $B_1, \ldots, B_n\subset L$ and $C_1 = X_{i_1}, \ldots, C_n = X_{i_n}$ for some $i_1 < i_2 < \ldots < i_n\in I$. Then by Property~\eqref{item:four}, there exists $B_{n+1}\in\mathcal{D}$ such that \[ B_{n+1}\subset\bigcap_{x\in X_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{i_n}}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr). \] It follows that $B_{n+1}\subset L$ and for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we have \[ B_{n+1}+C_k\subset A. \] Choose $i_{n+1}\in I$ that is sufficiently large such that \[ B_1\cup \cdots \cup B_n\cup B_{n+1}\subset F_{i_{n+1}} \] and set $C_{n+1} = X_{i_{n+1}}$. Then it follows from Property~\eqref{item:three} that for all $1 \leq k \leq n+1$, we have $$B_k+C_{n+1}\subset A, $$ completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Build intervals J_i rich in Q_i, use Bergelson's intersectivity lemma, then inductively choose B_n and C_n = X_{i_n}. The key step is the intersectivity lemma giving property (iv).

nodes.name: Sets Q_i
nodes.statement: Q_i = \bigcap_{x\in F_i}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon\Big\}.

nodes.name: Intersectivity conclusion
nodes.statement: \mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{k\in H}\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0.
nodes.label: eq:berg-cor

nodes.name: Density Ramsey version of B⊕B+t
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{D}\subset\{F\subset\mathbb{N}\colon 0 < |F|< \infty\}$ has the density Ramsey property, then is it true that for any $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)> 0$, there exist $t\in \mathbb{N}$ and disjoint $B_1, B_2, \ldots\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $B_i+B_j\subset A-t$ for all $i\neq j\in\mathbb{N}$?
nodes.label: thm_BBt_szemeredi

nodes.name: Measure preserving system
nodes.statement: The quadruple $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ is a \define{measure preserving system} if $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ is a probability space, and $T\colon X\to X$ is a measurable and measure preserving map.

nodes.name: Furstenberg Correspondence Principle
nodes.statement: As part of his proof of Szemer\'{e}di{}'s theorem, Furstenberg~\cite{Furstenberg-1977} introduced a general method, known as the \define{Correspondence Principle}, for translating a problem about finding configurations in sets of upper Banach density into a question of recurrence in measure preserving systems.

nodes.name: Set of recurrence
nodes.statement: A set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a \define{set of recurrence}~\cite{Furstenberg-book} if for any measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ and any $E\in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(E)>0$, there exist infinitely many $n\in R$ with $\mu(E\cap T^{-n}E)>0$.

nodes.name: Set of strong recurrence
nodes.statement: A set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a \define{set of strong recurrence}~\cite{bergelson} if for any measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ and any $E\in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(E)>0$ one has \[ \limsup_{n\in R} \mu(E\cap T^{-n}E)>0. \]

nodes.name: Strong recurrence is strictly stronger than recurrence
nodes.statement: Note that any set of strong recurrence is a set of recurrence, but the converse does not hold~\cite{forrest-1991}.
conclusions: any set of strong recurrence is a set of recurrence
the converse does not hold

nodes.name: Ordered sumsets from sets of strong recurrence
nodes.statement: Suppose that the set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a set of strong recurrence. Then for any $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$, there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset A$ such that \[ \{b+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A. \]
assumptions: Suppose that the set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a set of strong recurrence.
conclusions: there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset A$ such that
nodes.label: thm_sumset_recurrence

nodes.name: Theorem 3.32 cannot give unrestricted sumsets
nodes.statement: We note that for a set $R$ with Banach density zero, the conclusion can not be strengthened to finding the unrestricted sumset $\{b+c:b\in B, c\in C\}$, and the obstruction to such a configuration is given by \cref{ex_reverse_restricted_sumset_squares_is_false} (see also \cref{prop_B+Cindensity}).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.32
nodes.statement: Fix $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$. By the Furstenberg correspondence principle (see~\cite{Furstenberg-book}), there exist a measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ and a set $E\in\mathcal{B}$ such that $\mu(E)=\mathsf{d}^*(A)$ and \begin{equation} \mathsf{d}^*((A-n_1)\cap\ldots\cap (A-n_j))\geq \mu(T^{-n_1}E\cap\ldots\cap T^{-n_j}E) \end{equation} for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n_1,\ldots,n_j\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$. Since $R$ is a set of strong recurrence, the sequence of sets $E_n=E\cap T^{-n}E$ satisfies $\limsup_{n\in R}\mu(E_n)>0$. Applying Bergelson's intersectivity lemma~\cite[Corollary~2.4]{bergelson} to the collection $\{E_n:n\in R\}$, there exists an infinite subset $L\subset R$ such that for any finite nonempty set $F\subset L$, the intersection $\bigcap_{n\in F} E_n$ has positive measure. Combining this with~\eqref{eqn_furstenberg_correspondence_inequ}, we conclude that for any finite nonempty set $F\subset L$, the intersection \[ A\cap\biggl(\bigcap_{n\in F} (A-n)\biggr) \] has positive upper Banach density. In particular, this intersection is infinite and we use it to inductively construct the sets $B$ and $C$. Namely, let $\ell_1<\ell_2<\ldots$ be an enumeration of $L$ and choose $b_1:=\ell_1$ and then choose $c_1$ to be any element in the intersection $A\cap (A-b_1)$ with $c_1>b_1$. Let $b_2\in L$ be any element larger than $c_1$ and then choose $c_2$ to be any element in $A\cap (A-b_1)\cap (A-b_2)$ with $c_2>b_2$. Choose $b_3\in L$ larger than $c_2$ and take $c_3$ to be any element in the intersection $A\cap (A-b_1)\cap (A-b_2) \cap (A-b_3)$ with $c_3>b_3$. Continuing this procedure, we obtain sets $C\subset A$ and $B\subset R$ with $\{b+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: Furstenberg correspondence plus Bergelson's intersectivity lemma give L ⊂ R with positive-density intersections; then build B, C alternately.

nodes.name: Furstenberg correspondence inequality
nodes.statement: \mathsf{d}^*((A-n_1)\cap\ldots\cap (A-n_j))\geq \mu(T^{-n_1}E\cap\ldots\cap T^{-n_j}E)
nodes.label: eqn_furstenberg_correspondence_inequ

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.33
nodes.statement: Since the set of perfect squares is known to be a set of strong recurrence~\cite{Furstenberg-1977}, \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence} implies the following corollary, lending evidence towards a positive answer to \cref{q_sumset_sarkozy}.
nodes.statement_short: Squares form a set of strong recurrence, so apply Theorem 3.32.

nodes.name: Ordered sums with squares
nodes.statement: For any $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$, there exist infinite sets $B\subset \mathbb{N}$ and $C\subset A$ such that \[ \{b^2+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A. \]
conclusions: there exist infinite sets $B\subset \mathbb{N}$ and $C\subset A$ such that

nodes.name: Variant for arbitrary infinite R
nodes.statement: If the set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ in \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence} is only assumed to be infinite instead of a set of strong recurrence, then a similar argument (using Furstenberg Correspondence and Fatou's lemma) shows that for any $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$, there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that \[ \{b+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A. \]
assumptions: $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ in \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence} is only assumed to be infinite
conclusions: there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that

nodes.name: Recurrence is necessary
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is not hard to see that the notion of recurrence is a necessary condition for the stronger conclusion in the theorem.
conclusions: the notion of recurrence is a necessary condition for the stronger conclusion in the theorem

nodes.name: Recurrence instead of strong recurrence
nodes.statement: Does the conclusion of \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence} hold if we replace the assumption on $R$ being a set of strong recurrence by $R$ being a set of recurrence?
nodes.label: q:weak

nodes.name: Set of strong k-recurrence
nodes.statement: Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, a set $R\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a \define{set of strong $k$-recurrence} if for any measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ and any $E\in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(E)>0$ one has \[ \limsup_{n\in R} \mu(E\cap T^{-n}E\cap \ldots\cap T^{-kn})>0. \]

nodes.name: Sketch: modify proof of Theorem 3.32
nodes.statement: With slight modifications of the proof of \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence}, one can obtain the following generalization of \cref{thm_sumset_recurrence} involving sets of strong $k$-recurrence.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the proof of Theorem 3.32 to k-fold strong recurrence.

nodes.name: Ordered sumsets with arithmetic progressions from strong k-recurrence
nodes.statement: Suppose $R$ is a set of strong $k$-recurrence. Then for any $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that \[ \bigcup_{\ell=0}^k\{\ell b+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A. \]
assumptions: Suppose $R$ is a set of strong $k$-recurrence.
conclusions: there exist infinite sets $B\subset R$ and $C\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that
nodes.label: thm_restricted_different_sumset_szemeredi

nodes.name: Set of primes
nodes.statement: The set $\mathbb{P}$ of primes has zero density, and so neither Szemer\'{e}di{}'s theorem nor any of the results in \cref{sec:sumsets_integers} are applicable.

nodes.name: Green-Tao theorem
nodes.statement: However, in a major breakthrough, Green and Tao~\cite{Green_Tao08} proved the analog of Szemer\'{e}di{}'s theorem in the primes, showing that $\mathbb{P}$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
conclusions: $\mathbb{P}$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions

nodes.name: B+C in the primes
nodes.statement: The set of primes contains a sumset $B+C$ for some infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: The set of primes contains a sumset $B+C$ for some infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: q:bcprimes

nodes.name: Granville's conditional theorem
nodes.statement: Granville~\cite{Granville90} proved \cref{q:bcprimes} conditionally on the prime tuples conjecture of Dickson, Hardy and Littlewood~\cite{Dickson1904, Hardy-Littlewood23} (see \cref{conj_hardylittlewood} in Appendix~\ref{appendixDHL} for the statement).
assumptions: conditionally on the prime tuples conjecture of Dickson, Hardy and Littlewood
conclusions: proved \cref{q:bcprimes}

nodes.name: Zhang's bounded gaps theorem (sumset form)
nodes.statement: The fact that $\mathbb{P}$ contains a sumset $B+C$ where $B$ is infinite and $C$ has two elements is equivalent to Zhang's theorem~\cite{Zhang14} on bounded gaps in primes.
conclusions: $\mathbb{P}$ contains a sumset $B+C$ where $B$ is infinite and $C$ has two elements

nodes.name: Maynard-Polymath sumsets in the primes
nodes.statement: The subsequent work of Maynard~\cite{Maynard15} and Polymath 8~\cite{Polymath14} implies that for any size $k$, the primes contain a sumset $B+C$ for some infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and some set $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ with at least $k$ elements.
conclusions: for any size $k$, the primes contain a sumset $B+C$ for some infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and some set $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ with at least $k$ elements

nodes.name: Tao-Ziegler ordered sumsets in the primes
nodes.statement: Recently, Tao and Ziegler~\cite{TZ23} adapted Maynard's sieve to show that there are infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ such that the ordered sumset \[ \{ b + c : b \in B,~c \in C,~b < c \} \] is contained in the primes.
conclusions: there are infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ such that the ordered sumset

nodes.name: Tao-Ziegler conditional B⊕B in P-1
nodes.statement: They further show that, conditionally on the Dickson-Hardy-Littlewood conjecture, $\mathbb{P}-1$ contains a sumset of the form $\{b_1+b_2: b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1\neq b_2\}$ for some infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: $\mathbb{P}-1$ contains a sumset of the form $\{b_1+b_2: b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1\neq b_2\}$ for some infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: No shift of the primes contains an IP-set
nodes.statement: There is no sequence $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ and shift $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}+t\supseteq \mathsf{FS}\big(\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\big). \end{equation}
conclusions: There is no sequence $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ and shift $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
nodes.label: prop_noprimeshiftedIP

nodes.name: Shifted primes containing an IP-set
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}+t\supseteq \mathsf{FS}\big(\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\big).
nodes.label: eq_primestraus

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.2
nodes.statement: Suppose, for the sake of a contradiction, that $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfy~\eqref{eq_primestraus}. Then $p_n:=x_n-t$ is prime for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Find a set of indices $F\subset\mathbb{N}$ with size $|F|=p_1$ and $\min F>1$, such that every prime $p_i$ with $i\in F$ has the same congruence class $\bmod\,p_1$. Then on the one hand $$q:=(p_1+t)+\sum_{i\in F}(p_i+t)\in\mathbb{P}+t$$ by assumption. On the other hand, $q\equiv t\bmod p_1$, so $q-t$ is both a prime and a multiple of $p_1$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: sum p_1 primes in one residue class mod p_1 to get a multiple of p_1.

nodes.name: Finite sums sets in shifted primes
nodes.statement: For comparison, it follows from~\cite[Example 9]{Green_Tao10} that for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ the set $\mathbb{P}-1$ contains $\mathsf{FS}(\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\})$ for some set $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb{N}$ (and the same holds for $\mathbb{P}+1$).
conclusions: for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ the set $\mathbb{P}-1$ contains $\mathsf{FS}(\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\})$ for some set $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: Bounded finite sums in shifted primes
nodes.statement: For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $$\mathbb{P}-1\supset \left\{ \sum_{n \in F} n : F \subset B\textup{ with } 0< |F| \leq k \right\}.$$ The analogous statement holds with $\mathbb{P}-1$ replaced by $\mathbb{P}+1$.
conclusions: For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that
The analogous statement holds with $\mathbb{P}-1$ replaced by $\mathbb{P}+1$.
nodes.label: conjecture_primestrueHindman

nodes.name: Only shifts ±1 are possible
nodes.statement: Observe that the shift in \cref{conjecture_primestrueHindman} is fixed independent of $k$, and any shift other than $\pm1$ leads to a false statement.

nodes.name: Ordered B+C+D in the primes
nodes.statement: There exist infinite sets $B,C,D\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $$\mathbb{P}\supset \big\{b+c+d:b\in B,c\in C, d\in D;\, b<c<d \big\}.$$
conclusions: There exist infinite sets $B,C,D\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that
nodes.label: conjecture_orderedprimesBCD

nodes.name: Ordered B+C with C in P-1
nodes.statement: There exist infinite sets $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and $C\subset\mathbb{P}-1$ such that $$\mathbb{P}\supset \big\{b+c:b\in B,c\in C;\, b<c\big\}.$$
conclusions: There exist infinite sets $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and $C\subset\mathbb{P}-1$ such that
nodes.label: conjecture_orderedprimesCBC

nodes.name: Analog with B in P-1 follows from Tao-Ziegler
nodes.statement: We remark that the analogous statement to \cref{conjecture_orderedprimesCBC} where $B$ is required to be contained in $\mathbb{P}-1$, instead of $C$, follows from the results in~\cite{TZ23} (together with the fact that there exists an infinite admissible set contained in $\mathbb{P}-1$).
conclusions: follows from the results in~\cite{TZ23}

nodes.name: Sumsets force repeated gaps
nodes.statement: Whenever $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ contains $B+C$ with $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ infinite, the set $A$ must have infinitely many pairs of terms at the same distance.
conclusions: the set $A$ must have infinitely many pairs of terms at the same distance

nodes.name: No relative-density version of Conjecture 4.1
nodes.statement: Just as in~\cite[Remark~1.4]{TZ23} this precludes a version of \cref{q:bcprimes} that applies to subsets of $\mathbb{P}$ with positive relative density: one can remove a subset of zero relative density from $\mathbb{P}$ such that the resulting set no longer has bounded gaps, and hence no infinite sumset.

nodes.name: Positive density sets need not contain B⊕B+t with B primes
nodes.statement: By \cref{prop_B+Cindensity}, we know that not every set of positive density contains a sumset of the form $B\oplus B+t$ where $B$ is an infinite set of primes and $t\in\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: not every set of positive density contains a sumset of the form $B\oplus B+t$ where $B$ is an infinite set of primes and $t\in\mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: Prime sumsets in a Liouville level set
nodes.statement: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be the set of natural numbers that have an odd number of prime factors counting multiplicity. Is there an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{P}$ such that $B\oplus B\subset A$?

nodes.name: Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions
nodes.statement: For progressions of higher length, the best known bounds are due to Gowers~\cite{Gowers01}, but Erd\H{o}s{} conjectured that if the sum of the reciprocals of a set of integers diverges then the set contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
assumptions: the sum of the reciprocals of a set of integers diverges
conclusions: the set contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions

nodes.name: Sublinear growth guaranteeing B+C
nodes.statement: In other words, can one find a non-decreasing function $h\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $h(N)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ such that any set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with \begin{equation} |A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}|\geq \frac{N}{h(N)} \end{equation} contains $B+C$ for two infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Growth condition
nodes.statement: |A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}|\geq \frac{N}{h(N)}
nodes.label: eq:growth-rate

nodes.name: No sublinear growth rate guarantees B+C
nodes.statement: However, the answer to this question is negative, because for any such function $h$ there exists a set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ whose asymptotic growth rate is larger than $N/h(N)$ but the distance between consecutive elements in $A$ tends to infinity.
conclusions: the answer to this question is negative

nodes.name: Proof via repeated gaps
nodes.statement: Considering two distinct elements of $C$, it follows that the sumset $B+C$ of two infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ contains infinitely many pairs of numbers at the same distance, so such a set $A$ provides a counterexample.
nodes.statement_short: B+C contains infinitely many pairs at a common distance, impossible when gaps tend to infinity.

nodes.name: Zero-density set whose dense subsets contain B+C
nodes.statement: Is there a set $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ with upper Banach density $0$ such that for any subset $A\subset S$ with positive relative density, meaning that \[ \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{|S\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}>0, \] there exist infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $B+C\subset A$?
nodes.label: q_sos_4

nodes.name: Dense subsets avoiding shifted copies
nodes.statement: Is it true that if $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ has zero Banach density, there exists a subset $A\subset S$ with positive relative density such that for all but finitely many $t\in\mathbb{N}$, $A\setminus(A-t)$ has the same relative density (in $S$) as $A$.
nodes.label: q_sos_3

nodes.name: Positive answer to Question 4.8 refutes Question 4.7
nodes.statement: To see why a positive answer to \cref{q_sos_3} implies a negative answer to \cref{q_sos_4}, suppose that $Y_t:=A\setminus(A-t)$ has the same relative density as $A$ for all but finitely many $t\in\mathbb{N}$. Choosing $N_t$ sufficiently large, the set \[ Y:=A\setminus\bigcup_t \{a\geq N_t: a\in A-t\} \] also has positive relative density but no gap $t$ ``appears'' in $Y$ infinitely many times, so $Y$ cannot contain an infinite sumset.
nodes.statement_short: Delete from A the late elements of each shifted copy A-t to get a dense Y with no repeated gaps.

nodes.name: Host's example
nodes.statement: In~\cite{Host}, Host exhibits an example of a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ such that whenever $B+C\subset A$, both $\mathsf{d}^*(B)=0$ and $\mathsf{d}^*(C)=0$.

nodes.name: Growth rate of summands
nodes.statement: Given $\delta>0$, is there a non-decreasing function $\mathcal{H}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathcal{H}(N)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ satisfying the following: for any set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\underline{\mathsf{d}}(A)\geq \delta$ there exist $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ with \[ \min\bigl\{|B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}|,\,|C\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}| \bigr\}\geq \mathcal{H}(N) \] for all sufficiently large $N$ and such that $B+C\subset A$.
nodes.label: q_quant_growth_B+C_in_A

nodes.name: Erdős-Galvin theorem
nodes.statement: In a similar direction, a result of Erd\H{o}s{} and Galvin~\cite{erdos_galvin} states that for any function $\mathcal{H}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathcal{H}(N)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ there is a 2-coloring of $\mathbb{N}$ such that whenever the IP-set $\mathsf{FS}(B)$ is monochromatic, one has $|B\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\leq\mathcal{H}(N)$.
conclusions: there is a 2-coloring of $\mathbb{N}$ such that whenever the IP-set $\mathsf{FS}(B)$ is monochromatic, one has $|B\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\leq\mathcal{H}(N)$

nodes.name: Finitary sumset size φ(δ,N)
nodes.statement: There is a similar regime that is worth exploring: given $\delta>0$ and $N\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\phi(\delta,N)$ denote the largest integer such that any set $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\geq \delta N$ contains $B+C$, where $B,C\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfy $\min\{|B|,|C|\}\geq \phi(\delta,N)$.

nodes.name: φ(δ,N) tends to infinity
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to show that $\phi(\delta,N)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ for any fixed $\delta>0$.
conclusions: $\phi(\delta,N)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ for any fixed $\delta>0$

nodes.name: φ(δ,N) grows like log N
nodes.statement: For every $\delta>0$, \[ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\delta,N)}{\log N}<\infty\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\delta,N)}{\log N}>0. \]
conclusions: \[ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\delta,N)}{\log N}<\infty\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\delta,N)}{\log N}>0. \]
nodes.label: conjecture_phiislog

nodes.name: Heuristic for φ(δ,N) ≈ log N
nodes.statement: Given $\delta>0$, $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A\subset[N]$ with $|A|\geq\delta N$, pick $B\subset[N]$ uniformly at random with $|B|=\varepsilon\log N$, for some small positive $\varepsilon$. Then the expected value of the cardinality of $C:=\bigcap_{b\in B}(A-b)$ is $|C|\approx\delta^{\varepsilon\log N}N=N^{\varepsilon\log\delta+1}\gg\log N$. This shows that $\phi(\delta,N)\gg\log N$. For the converse estimate, one can take $A$ itself to be a random set, and then for any $B$ with size $|B|=\theta\log N$, for some parameter $\theta>0$, the expected value of the cardinality of $C:=\bigcap_{b\in B}(A-b)$ should be $|C|\approx\delta^{\theta\log N}N\ll\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Random B of size ε log N leaves many common translates; a random A shows θ log N is too many.

nodes.name: Limit of φ(δ,N)/log N
nodes.statement: Does the limit \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi(\delta,N)}{\log N} \] exist, and if so, what is it?

nodes.name: φ with δ_N → 0
nodes.statement: Is $\displaystyle\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\phi\big(\delta_N,N\big)}{\log N}>0$ for some sequence $\delta_N\to0$ as $N\to\infty$? Can one take $\delta_N=1/\log N$?

nodes.name: Random set with probabilities p_n
nodes.statement: Let $(p_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence taking values in $[0,1]$ and consider the random set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ defined such that the event $n\in A$ has probability $p_n$ and these events are independent.

nodes.name: Dense random sets contain sumsets
nodes.statement: If the probabilities $p_n$ are not sufficiently small, then $A$ almost surely contains arbitrarily long intervals and hence also infinite sumsets.
assumptions: the probabilities $p_n$ are not sufficiently small
conclusions: $A$ almost surely contains arbitrarily long intervals and hence also infinite sumsets

nodes.name: Borel-Cantelli argument
nodes.statement: More precisely, if $(p_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a decreasing sequence and for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}p_n\cdot n^{\varepsilon}\to\infty \] then for every $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, the probability that the interval $[n+1,n+k]$ is contained in $A$ is $\prod_{i=1}^kp_{n+i}$, which is approximately equal to $p_n^k$. Since for disjoint intervals these events are independent and eventually have probability larger than $1/n$, by the second Borel-Cantelli lemma it follows that $A$ contains infinitely many intervals of length $k$ almost surely. Since this holds for every $k$, the set $A$ is thick (see \cref{def:thick_synd_ps}) almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Intervals [n+1,n+k] lie in A with probability ≈ p_n^k; second Borel-Cantelli gives infinitely many, so A is thick.

nodes.name: Sparse random sets avoid B+F
nodes.statement: On the other hand, suppose that \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}p_n\cdot n^\varepsilon = 0 \] for some $\varepsilon>0$. Then for some $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we have that $p_n\ll n^{-1/k}$. Then for any set $F\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $|F|=k$, the probability that $A$ contains infinitely many shifts of $F$ is $0$ and hence almost surely $A$ does not contain the configuration $B+F$ for any infinite set $B\subset \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: If p_n n^ε → 0, then a.s. A contains only finitely many shifts of any k-set F, so no B+F.

nodes.name: Sumsets in A_x = {n : {n^γ x} ≤ 1/log n}
nodes.statement: Fix $\gamma>0$ and, for each $x\in\mathbb{R}$, let $A_x:=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\{n^\gamma x\}\leq1/\log n\}$. For which values of $\gamma$ is it true that for almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the set $A_x$ contains a sumset $B+C$ for infinite sets $B, C\subset\mathbb{N}$?

nodes.name: A_x thick for γ<1
nodes.statement: We note that for $\gamma<1$, the set $A_x$ is thick for almost every $x$ and hence contains a sumset.
conclusions: for $\gamma<1$, the set $A_x$ is thick for almost every $x$ and hence contains a sumset

nodes.name: A_x has no sumset for integer γ
nodes.statement: On the other hand, when $\gamma$ is an integer one can show that for every irrational $x$ the set $A_x$ cannot contain an infinite sumset.
conclusions: when $\gamma$ is an integer one can show that for every irrational $x$ the set $A_x$ cannot contain an infinite sumset

nodes.name: Multiplicative Følner sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence $(\Phi_N)_{N \in \mathbb{N}}$ of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is a \define{multiplicative F\o{}lner{} sequence} if \[ \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{|\Phi_N \cap t\Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} = 1 \] for all $t \in \mathbb{N}$ where $t \Phi_N = \{ tn : n \in \Phi_N \}$.

nodes.name: Product sets in multiplicatively dense sets
nodes.statement: It is an immediate consequence of~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{MRR} that if $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has positive upper density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ for multiplication, then $A$ contains a product set \[ BC = \{ bc : b \in B, c \in C \} \] for some infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has positive upper density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ for multiplication
conclusions: $A$ contains a product set

nodes.name: Multiplicative B+B+t conjecture
nodes.statement: If $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has positive density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence for multiplication, then it contains $\{b_1b_2t:b_1\neq b_2\}$ for some infinite set $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has positive density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence for multiplication
conclusions: it contains $\{b_1b_2t:b_1\neq b_2\}$ for some infinite set $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: Ackelsberg's multiplicative counterexample
nodes.statement: The recent work of Acklesberg~\cite[Theorem 1.4]{ackelsberg} shows that this is false. He constructs an explicit example with local obstructions that is an adaptation of the Straus example (\cref{example_straus}) to the multiplicative setting.
conclusions: shows that this is false

nodes.name: Aperiodic set
nodes.statement: Say that $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ is \define{aperiodic} if \begin{equation} \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \boldsymbol{1}_A(n)e(\alpha n) =0 \quad\textup{ for all } \alpha\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z} \end{equation} where $e(\alpha n) = e^{2 \pi i \alpha n}$.

nodes.name: Aperiodicity condition
nodes.statement: \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \boldsymbol{1}_A(n)e(\alpha n) =0 \quad\textup{ for all } \alpha\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}

nodes.statement: Fix $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ that has positive density and is aperiodic. Are there infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $B+C \subset A$ and $BC \subset A$?

nodes.name: Partition regularity of B+C and BC
nodes.statement: Is it true that for every finite partition of $\mathbb{N}$, one of the sets in the partition contains $B+C$ and $BC$ for some infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$?

nodes.name: Aperiodicity is needed

conclusions: the answer is negative due to local obstructions

nodes.name: B+C and BC+1 in sets of positive logarithmic density
nodes.statement: Suppose $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ has positive upper logarithmic density. Are there infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $B+C \subset A$ and $BC+1 \subset A$?

nodes.statement: Does every syndetic set $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ contain a product set $BC$ for infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$?
nodes.label: question_syndeticproducts

nodes.name: Double Følner sequence
nodes.statement: To measure density in $\mathbb{Q}$ we make use of a \emph{double F\o{}lner{} sequence} $\Phi=(\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$, as introduced in~\cite[Definition 1.3]{Bergelson_Moreira17}; this means that $\Phi$ is simultaneously a F\o{}lner{} sequence in group $(\mathbb{Q},+)$ and in the group $(\mathbb{Q}^*,\times)$.

nodes.name: Sums and products in Q
nodes.statement: Let $A\subset\mathbb{Q}$ have $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)>0$ for some double F\o{}lner{} sequence $\Phi$. Are there infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{Q}$ such that $B+C \subset A$ and $BC \subset A$?

nodes.name: Hindman's sums and products partition question
nodes.statement: Does there exist a partition of $\mathbb{N}$ into two sets such that neither of them contains an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ together with \[ \{b_1+b_2: b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1\neq b_2\}\cup\{b_1b_2: b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1\neq b_2\}? \]
nodes.label: q_hindman80_31_Qa

nodes.statement: Hindman~\cite{Hindman80} showed this question has a positive answer if one instead considers partitions of $\mathbb{N}$ into seven sets.
conclusions: this question has a positive answer if one instead considers partitions of $\mathbb{N}$ into seven sets

nodes.statement: For any finite coloring of $\mathbb{N}^2$ there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{equation} \{(b_1,b_2): b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1<b_2\} \end{equation}is monochromatic.
conclusions: there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that

nodes.name: Fiber A_n
nodes.statement: Given $A\subset\mathbb{N}^2$, we write $A_n=\{m\in\mathbb{N}: (n,m)\in A\}$ for the fiber of $A$ with first coordinate $n$.

nodes.name: Necessary condition for (21)
nodes.statement: A necessary condition for $A$ to satisfy~\eqref{eqn:BBcart} is that there are infinitely many vertical fibers $A_n$ such that any finite subcollection of them has infinite intersection.
conclusions: there are  infinitely many vertical fibers $A_n$ such that any finite subcollection of them has infinite intersection

nodes.name: Full-density set with finite fibers
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi=(\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a F\o{}lner{} sequence in $\mathbb{N}^2$ (see \cref{sec:amenable} for the definition). Then there exists a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ and such that each vertical fiber $A_n$ is finite. In particular, any such $A$ cannot satisfy~\eqref{eqn:BBcart}. For each $j\in\mathbb{N}$, using the F\o lner property, we choose the smallest $N_j$ such that for any $N>N_j$, the first $j$ columns of $\Phi_N$ account for less than $1/j$ of the total cardinality of $\Phi_N$. More precisely, if $N> N_j$, then \begin{equation*} \sum_{n>j}\big|(\Phi_N)_n\big|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j). \end{equation*} Let $M_j=\max\{m:(j,m)\in\Phi_N,N\leq N_j\}=\max\bigcup_{N\leq N_j}(\Phi_N)_j$ and take $A$ to be the set described in terms of its columns by $A_j=\{1,\dots,M_j\}$. Note that if $n\geq j$ and $N\leq N_j$, then $A_j\supset(\Phi_N)_j$. It follows that for $N\in[N_j,N_{j+1}]$, $$|A\cap\Phi_N|=\sum_n|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|\geq\sum_{n>j}|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|=\sum_{n>j}|(\Phi_N)_n|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j),$$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: For any Følner sequence in N^2, a set with finite columns of full density, so no Cartesian configuration (21).

nodes.name: Full density with finite vertical fibers
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi=(\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a F\o{}lner{} sequence in $\mathbb{N}^2$ (see \cref{sec:amenable} for the definition). Then there exists a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ and such that each vertical fiber $A_n$ is finite.
assumptions: Let $\Phi=(\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a F\o{}lner{} sequence in $\mathbb{N}^2$ (see \cref{sec:amenable} for the definition).
conclusions: there exists a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ and such that each vertical fiber $A_n$ is finite

nodes.name: Construction of the column set
nodes.statement: For each $j\in\mathbb{N}$, using the F\o lner property, we choose the smallest $N_j$ such that for any $N>N_j$, the first $j$ columns of $\Phi_N$ account for less than $1/j$ of the total cardinality of $\Phi_N$. More precisely, if $N> N_j$, then \begin{equation*} \sum_{n>j}\big|(\Phi_N)_n\big|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j). \end{equation*} Let $M_j=\max\{m:(j,m)\in\Phi_N,N\leq N_j\}=\max\bigcup_{N\leq N_j}(\Phi_N)_j$ and take $A$ to be the set described in terms of its columns by $A_j=\{1,\dots,M_j\}$. Note that if $n\geq j$ and $N\leq N_j$, then $A_j\supset(\Phi_N)_j$. It follows that for $N\in[N_j,N_{j+1}]$, $$|A\cap\Phi_N|=\sum_n|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|\geq\sum_{n>j}|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|=\sum_{n>j}|(\Phi_N)_n|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j),$$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Choose column heights M_j from the Følner sets so that the first j columns are negligible; then A has density 1.

Does there exist an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ and an element $t\in\mathbb{N}^2$ satisfying~\eqref{eqn:BBcart}?

nodes.statement: \liminf_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_n) >0

nodes.name: Question 5.10 implies Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: Using the map $(x,y) \mapsto x+y$, one can show that a positive answer to \cref{q_bxbxt2} implies \cref{thm_BBt}.

nodes.name: Hernández Castro's example
nodes.statement: Take $1<c<c'<c''<2$ and define \[ X=\mathbb{N} \cap \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[4^{n},c\cdot4^{n}\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad Y=\mathbb{N} \cap \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[c'4^{n},c''\cdot4^{n}\right), \] and take $A=X\times Y$. Note that for every integer $t\geq 0$ the intersection $X\cap (Y-t)$ is finite, implying that no shift of $A$ can contain a set of the form $\{(b_1,b_2): b_1,b_2\in B,~b_1<b_2\}$ for some infinite $B \subset \mathbb{N}$. Yet, there is $\delta>0$ such that $\underline{\mathsf{d}}(A_n)>\delta$ holds for a set of $n\in\mathbb{N}$ that has positive lower density.
nodes.label: ex_felipe

nodes.name: Ordered Cartesian products under limsup fiber density
nodes.statement: If $A\subset\mathbb{N}^2$ satisfies $\limsup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_n) >0$ for some F\o{}lner{} sequence $\Phi$, then there exist infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $\{(b,c): b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A$.
conclusions: there exist infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $\{(b,c): b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A$
nodes.label: q_bxc_restircted

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.12
nodes.statement: By assumption on the set $A$, there are $a > 0$ and $n(1)<n(2)<\ldots\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_{n(i)}) \ge a$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. It follows from~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{bergelson} that, after possibly passing to a sub-F\o{}lner{} sequence, there is a subsequence $r(1), r(2), \ldots$ of the sequence $n(1),n(2),\ldots$ with \[ \mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_{r(1)} \cap A_{r(2)} \cap \cdots \cap A_{r(i)}) > 0 \] for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. Inductively choose $b(i)$ and $c(i)$ with $c(i) \in A_{b(1)} \cap \cdots \cap A_{b(i)}$ and $b(i+1) > c(i) > b(i)$. Taking $B = \{b(i) : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $C = \{ c(i) : i \in \mathbb{N} \}$, the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Bergelson's intersectivity lemma on dense fibers, then choose b(i), c(i) alternately.

nodes.name: No full Cartesian product in general
nodes.statement: A tantalizing possibility is to upgrade the conclusion of \cref{q_bxc_restircted} to $A\supset B\times C$, but a counterexample is the set $A=\{(n,m):n<m\}$ which can not contain such a Cartesian product with both $B$ and $C$ infinite.

nodes.name: Symmetric set without Cartesian products
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the set $ \big\{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^2: \max\{r,s\}~\text{is even},~\min\{r,s\}~\text{is odd}\big\}, $ which is a symmetric subset of $\mathbb{N}^2$ whose density equals $1/4$ with respect to any F\o{}lner{} sequence in $\mathbb{N}^2$. Moreover, $d_\Phi(A_n)=1/2$ for every odd $n$ and every F\o lner sequence $\Phi$ in $\mathbb{N}$. However, there are no infinite sets $B,C \subset \mathbb{N}$ such that $B \times C\subset A$.
nodes.label: example_evenoddproduct

nodes.statement: When $G=\mathbb{Z}$, we can restrict the value of $t$ to lie in $\{0,1\}$ (see \cref{prop:equivalences-for-shifts}).
conclusions: we can restrict the value of $t$ to lie in $\{0,1\}$

nodes.name: Which shifts suffice in abelian groups
nodes.statement: Assuming that \cref{q:bbt_abelian} holds, what values of the shift $t$ suffice?

nodes.name: t=0 suffices in direct sums of Z/3Z
nodes.statement: When $G$ is the direct sum of infinitely many copies of $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ one can always take $t=0$ because all elements in this group are divisible by $2$.
conclusions: one can always take $t=0$

nodes.name: t=0 fails in direct sums of Z/2Z
nodes.statement: In contrast, if $G$ is the direct sum of infinitely many copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ then one can consider the set of all elements in $G$ whose Hamming distance to the origin is odd, yielding a set of positive density that does not contain $B\oplus B$ for infinite $B$, showing that one can not always take $t=0$ in this case.

nodes.name: Følner sequence in an amenable group
nodes.statement: Recall that amenability of a countable group $(G,\cdot)$ is characterized by the existence of a \define{F\o{}lner{} sequence}: a sequence $N \mapsto \Phi_N$ of finite, nonempty subsets of $G$ satisfying \[ \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{|\Phi_N \cap g \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} = 1 = \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{|\Phi_N g \cap \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} \] for all $g \in G$.
nodes.genus: sequence $N \mapsto \Phi_N$ of finite, nonempty subsets of $G$

nodes.name: Upper density along a Følner sequence in G
nodes.statement: Given a F\o{}lner{} sequence, one speaks of the upper density of a set $A \subset G$ with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence \[ \overline{\mathsf{d}}_\Phi(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{|A \cap \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} \] and can enquire about those configurations that are guaranteed in any set whose upper density is positive.

nodes.name: Moreira-Richter-Robertson theorem in amenable groups
nodes.statement: The main result of~\cite{MRR} holds in this context: every subset of a countable, amenable group with positive upper density contains the product \[ B \cdot C = \{ bc : b \in B, c \in C \} \] of two infinite sets $B,C \subset G$ (\cite[Theorem 1.3]{MRR}).
conclusions: every subset of a countable, amenable group with positive upper density contains the product

nodes.name: Ordered products in amenable groups
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a countable amenable group and $A\subset G$ has positive upper-density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence, is there an injective sequence $b:\mathbb{N}\to G$ and $t \in G$ with \[ \{ b(i) b(j) : i < j \} \] contained in $t^{-1}A$?

nodes.statement: For which countable amenable groups $G$ is it true that whenever $A\subset G$ has positive upper density with respect to a F\o{}lner{} sequence, there are infinite sets $B,C,D \subset G$ with $BCD \subset A$?

nodes.statement: By a \define{left F\o{}lner{}} sequence we mean a sequence $N \mapsto \Phi_N$ of finite, nonempty subsets of $G$ satisfying \[ \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{|\Phi_N \cap g \Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|} = 1 \] for all $g \in G$.

nodes.name: Left and right finite products sets
nodes.statement: In a non-abelian group $(G,\cdot)$ there are two versions of finite sumsets: given a sequence $n \mapsto g(n)$ in $G$ one can define \begin{align*} \mathsf{FPL}(g) &= \{ g(i_1) \cdots g(i_r) : i_1 < \cdots < i_r \} \\ \mathsf{FPR}(g) &= \{ g(i_r) \cdots g(i_1) : i_r > \cdots > i_1 \} \end{align*} for the left and right finite products sets defined by $g$.

nodes.name: Partition regularity of BC in groups
nodes.statement: Fix a countable group $(G,\cdot)$. Does every finite partition of $G$ have a cell that contains $BC$ for infinite sets $B,C \subset G$?

nodes.name: Product Følner sequence Φ^d
nodes.statement: Given a F\o{}lner{} sequence $N \mapsto \Phi_N$ on $G$ write $\Phi^d$ for the F\o{}lner{} sequence $N \mapsto \Phi_N \times \cdots \times \Phi_N$ on $G^d$.

nodes.name: Austin's corners theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G^d$ be the direct product of $d$ copies of an amenable group $(G,\cdot)$ and let $N\mapsto \Phi_N$ be a left F\o{}lner{} sequence in $G$. If $A\subset G^d$ satisfies $\overline{\mathsf{d}}_{\Phi^d}(A)>0$ then \[ \begin{split} \overline{\mathsf{d}}_{\Phi}\Bigl(\bigl\{& g\in G: \text{there exists } (a_1,a_2\ldots, a_d)\in G^d~\text{such that}~(a_1,a_2\ldots,a_d), \\ &(ga_1,a_2\ldots,a_d),(ga_1,ga_2\ldots,a_d),\ldots, (ga_1,\ldots,ga_d)\in A\bigr\}\Bigr)>0. \end{split} \]
assumptions: Let $G^d$ be the direct product of $d$ copies of an amenable group $(G,\cdot)$ and let $N\mapsto \Phi_N$ be a left F\o{}lner{} sequence in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Positive-density subsets of G^d contain many corner configurations (a, ga_1, …) with g ranging over a set of positive density.

nodes.name: Ultrafilter
nodes.statement: An \emph{ultrafilter} is a non-empty collection $\ultra{p}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ closed under intersections and supersets which satisfies $A\notin\ultra{p}\iff(\mathbb{N}\setminus A)\in\ultra{p}$ for every $A\subset\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Sum of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Proof via conditional expectation and Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: To see this, combine \[ \langle T^n f, g \rangle = \int \mathbb{E}(T^n f \cdot \overline{g} \mid \mathcal{I} ) \, d\mu, \] where $\mathbb{E}(\cdot \mid \mathcal{I})$ denotes the conditional expectation on the invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{I}$, with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to obtain \begin{align*} \left( \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N | \langle T^n f, g \rangle| \right)^2 & \le \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \int | \mathbb{E}( T^n f \cdot \overline{g} \mid \mathcal{I} ) |^2 \,d \mu \\ = \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N & \lim_{M \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \int T^n f \cdot \overline{g} \cdot T^{n+m} \overline{f} \cdot T^m g \,d \mu \end{align*} then note that this last expression is zero whenever the second Host-Kra seminorm of $f$ is zero by~\cite[Theorem~8.13]{HK-book}.

The limit as $M \to \infty$ of the quantity inside $| \cdot |$ is non-negative, and so we may dispense in the limit with the absolute values. Then taking the Ces\`{a}ro{} average in $N$, we obtain \begin{align*} & \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \left| \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n) g(j) \right|^2 \\ \le & \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \lim_{M \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n+m) g(j+m) f(j+n) g(j) \end{align*} and H\"{o}lder{}'s inequality shows that this last term is zero whenever $\ghkn{f}_\un{2}{\Phi}$ equals zero.

nodes.name: Admissible set
nodes.statement: A (finite or infinite) set $H\subset\mathbb{N}$ is called \emph{admissible} if for every prime $p\in\mathbb{P}$ there exists $i=i(p)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that no element of $H$ is congruent to $i\bmod p$.

nodes.name: Dickson-Hardy-Littlewood conjecture

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.3
nodes.statement:
Given $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$ denote by $[n]:=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ and denote by $[n]^{<k}:=\{F\subset[n]:|F|<k\}$. We stress that $[n]^{<k}$ includes the empty set. Our goal (cf.\ \cref{conjecture_primestrueHindman}) is to construct, for a given fixed $k\in\mathbb{N}$, a strictly increasing sequence $b:\mathbb{N}	o\mathbb{N}$ such that  egin{equation}  orall n\in\mathbb{N},\  orall F\in[n]^{<k+1},\ F
eq\varnothing, \qquad \sum_{i\in F}b(i)\in\mathbb{P}-1. \end{equation} We construct additionally, for each prime $p$, some $x_p\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ such that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in\mathbb{P}$,  egin{equation} p<k2^{n}\ \Rightarrow\ b(n)\equiv x_p mod p \end{equation} and  egin{equation}  orall F\in[n]^{<k},\  orall\ell\leq k-|F|,\qquad p
ot|\left(1+\ell x_p+\sum_{i\in F}b(i)ight) \end{equation} both hold. Let $b(1)\in\mathbb{P}-1$ be divisible by each prime $p< 2k$, and set $x_p:=0$ for those primes. That such a $b(1)$ exists follows from Dirichlet's theorem. Suppose now that $m>1$ and we have chosen $b(1),\dots,b(m-1)$ and $(x_p)_{p<k2^{m-1}}$ satisfying~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimesb}, \eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} and~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} for all $n<m$ and each prime $p<k2^{m-1}$. For each prime $p\in(k2^{m-1},k2^{m})$ choose an arbitrary $x_p$ such that  egin{equation}  orall F\in[m-1]^{<k},\  orall\ell\leq k,\qquad p
ot|\left(1+\ell x_p+\sum_{i\in F}b(i)ight). \end{equation} Note that there are at most $k2^{m-1}$ values of $x_p mod p$ that do \emph{not} satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}; therefore for each $p>k2^{m-1}$ we can choose a value of $x_p$ that does satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}. Observe that this choice of $x_p$ satisfies~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} for all $n<m$ and $p<k2^{m}$. Let $q=\prod_{p<k2^{m}}p$ and use the Chinese remainder theorem to find $a\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a\equiv x_p mod p$ for every $p<k2^{m}$. Next let $$H:=\left\{1+\sum_{i\in F}b(i):F\in[m-1]^{<k}ight\}.$$ Note that $|H|\leq 2^{m-1}$. It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} that for each $p<2^{m-1}\leq k2^{m-1}$, $|\{b(n) mod p:n\leq m-1\}|\leq1+\log_2(p/k)< p$ and hence that $H$ is an admissible set. It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} that $(a+h,q)=1$ for every $h\in H$. In view of \cref{lemma_DHLinprogressions}, there exists $b(m)>b(m-1)$ such that $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ and $b(m)\equiv a mod q$. From $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimesb} holds with $n=m$. From $b(m)\equiv a mod q$ and the fact that $a\equiv x_p mod p$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} holds with $n=m$. Finally, from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} holds with $n=m$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$.

nodes.name: Second implies first; third implies second
nodes.statement: Clearly the second statement implies the first. To see how the third statement implies the second, let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ and find $t\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ such that $A':=A\cap (k\mathbb{N}+t)$ has $\mathsf{d}^*(A')>0$. Then $A'-t\subset k\mathbb{N}$ and by the third statement there exists an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $B^{\oplus k}\subset A'-t$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Searching for a density version of Hindman's theorem
nodes.statement_short: (2)⇒(1) is clear; for (3)⇒(2) restrict A to a dense residue class mod k and shift.

nodes.name: First implies third
nodes.statement: To show that the first statement implies the third, let $A\subset k\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$ and, using the first statement, find $t\geq0$ and an infinite set $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $B^{\oplus k}+t\subset A\subset k\mathbb{N}$. Now $B$ must contain $k$ elements which are all congruent modulo $k$, and therefore their sum is a multiple of $k$. It follows that $t=k\tilde{t}$ for some $\tilde{t}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Letting $\tilde{B}=B+\tilde{t}$ we conclude that $\tilde{B}^{\oplus k}\subset A$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Searching for a density version of Hindman's theorem
nodes.statement_short: (1)⇒(3): k elements congruent mod k force t to be a multiple of k; absorb t/k into B.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: By \cref{thm:MRR}, there exist infinite sets $B,C\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that $B+C\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: Get B+C ⊂ A from Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Shift into P and Q
nodes.statement: Since $P$ and $Q$ are syndetic, we can find shifts $p,q\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $(P+p)\cap B$ and $(Q+q)\cap C$ are both infinite. Take \begin{align*} P' &= ((P+p)\cap B)-p=P\cap(B-p) \\ Q' &= ((Q+q)\cap C)-q=Q\cap(C-q) \end{align*} and $t=p+q$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift P, Q to meet B, C infinitely often and define P', Q', t.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We have that $P'+Q'\subset B+C-t\subset A-t$.
nodes.statement_short: P'+Q' lies in A-t.

nodes.name: (2)⇒(1) from MRR
nodes.statement: The implication $ \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} \Rightarrow \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} $ follows from a careful analysis of the proof in~\cite{MRR} (or the proofs in~\cite{Host} and in~\cite{KMRR}).

nodes.name: Construct A avoiding a thickened W
nodes.statement: The proof of $ \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} \Rightarrow \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment} $ is by construction. If $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(W)=0$ we can find a slowly growing sequence $f\colon \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n)=\infty$ and such that the set \[ \tilde W := \bigcup_{w\in W}[w-f(w),w+f(w)] \] still has $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(\tilde W)=0$. Letting $A=\mathbb{N}\setminus\tilde W$ we see that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$.

nodes.name: C must be finite
nodes.statement: Whenever $A$ contains a sumset $B+C$ and $C\subset W$, if $b\in B$ and $w\in W$ are such that $f(w)>b$, then we cannot have $w\in C$ (as $w+b\notin A$). It follows that $C$ must be finite, finishing the proof.

nodes.name: Assume W not syndetic
nodes.statement: For the final direction $ \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment3} \Rightarrow \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment3} $, assume that $W$ is not syndetic and so for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there exist $a_n,b_n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $|b_n-a_n|\geq 2n$ and such that $W\cap [a_n,b_n]=\varnothing$.
