nodes.name: Build thick A
nodes.statement: Then the set $A=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} [a_{n}+n,b_{n}]$ is a thick set with the property that any shift of it $A-t$ has finite intersection with $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Union of shortened gaps gives a thick A each shift of which meets W finitely.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore one can not find infinite sets $B\subset\mathbb{N}$, $C\subset W$ such that $B+C\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: No B+C ⊂ A with C ⊂ W infinite.

nodes.name: Easy direction; plan
nodes.statement: The implication $ \eqref{item1ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment2} \Rightarrow \eqref{item2ofthepropositiononequivalentcontainment2} $ is obvious. The converse implication uses Ramsey's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: (1)⇒(2) is obvious; the converse uses Ramsey's theorem.

nodes.name: Color pairs
nodes.statement: Assuming $W$ is infinite and $A$ is syndetic, find $r\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cup(A-1)\cup\cdots\cup(A-r)=\mathbb{N}$. Then color each pair $\{w_1,w_2\}$ of elements of $W$ with the color $i\in\{0,\dots,r\}$ such that $w_1+w_2+i\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: Color pairs of W by the shift i putting their sum in A.

nodes.name: Apply Ramsey
nodes.statement: Using Ramsey's theorem one can extract an infinite subset $W'\subset W$ such that every pair $\{w_1,w_2\}\subset W'$ has the same color $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Ramsey gives an infinite monochromatic W'.

nodes.name: Split and conclude
nodes.statement: Next split $W'$ into two disjoint infinite sets $W'=C\cup B'$ and let $B=B'+i$. It follows that $C\subset W$ and $B+C\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: Split W' into C and B' and shift B' by i.

nodes.name: Fix data
nodes.statement: Fix $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ infinite and let $b_1\in B$ be arbitrary. Let $b\in B$ be sufficiently large depending on $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,t$ and $b_1$. Let $m_1=\lfloor\lambda_1b_1+\lambda_2b\rfloor+t$ and $m_2=\lfloor\lambda_1b+\lambda_2b_1\rfloor+t$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix t, B, b_1, large b, and define m_1, m_2.

nodes.name: Compare m1 and m2
nodes.statement: Note that $\rho^2m_1\approx m_2$ as $b\to\infty$, so \[ \rho m_1<m_2 <\rho^3m_1 \] if we choose $b$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: ρ m_1 < m_2 < ρ^3 m_1 for large b.

nodes.name: Colors differ
nodes.statement: Taking $\log_{\rho}$ on each term we conclude that \[ \log_{\rho}(m_2)\in\Big(\log_{\rho}(m_1)+1,\log_{\rho}(m_1)+3\Big) \] and after taking floors and reducing modulo 3 we get $\chi(m_1)\neq\chi(m_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Taking logs and floors mod 3 gives different colors.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Suppose $t,m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ satisfy~\eqref{eq_runningoutoflabels}. We show that $B$ can not be infinite.
nodes.statement_short: Assume (12) and aim to show B is finite.

nodes.name: Locate the sums
nodes.statement: Indeed, take $b_0\in B$ and suppose that there exists $b\in B$ arbitrarily large, depending on $b_0$. Since $b_0+mb+t\in A$ and $mb_0+b+t\in A$, there exist $n,n'\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $b_0+mb+t\in[x_n,\tfrac32x_n]$ and $mb_0+b+t\in[x_{n'},\tfrac32x_{n'}]$. Since $b>b_0$ and $m\geq1$, we have $n\geq{n'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick b_0 and large b; the two sums lie in intervals n ≥ n'.

nodes.name: Case n = n'
nodes.statement: If $n={n'}$, then $$b_0+mb+t\leq\tfrac32(mb_0+b+t)\iff b\leq\frac{3m-2}{2m-3}b_0+\frac{t}{2m-3},$$ but for large enough $b$ this is not possible.
nodes.statement_short: Same interval contradicts largeness of b.

nodes.name: Case n > n'
nodes.statement: If $n>{n'}$ then $$b_0+mb+t\geq x_n>4x_{n'}^2>2x_{n'}(mb_0+b+t)>(mb_0+b+t)^2>b^2,$$ whence $b(b-m)<b_0+t$, and again this is not possible for sufficiently large $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Growth of x_n gives b(b-m) < b_0+t, impossible.

nodes.name: Residues
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose $\{b,b'\}\subset A_m-t$. Then $b,b'\equiv-1-t\bmod2m$ and so $b+b'\equiv-2-2t \bmod2m$.
nodes.statement_short: b, b' ≡ -1-t and b+b' ≡ -2-2t mod 2m.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $-1-t\equiv-2-2t\bmod2m$ only holds when $t\equiv-1\bmod2m$, it follows that $b+b'\notin A_m-t$.
nodes.statement_short: These residues differ for t < m, so b+b' ∉ A_m - t.

nodes.name: A is weakly mixing
nodes.statement: Since $\ghkn{\boldsymbol{1}_A-\mathsf{d}_ \Phi(A)}_\un{2}{\Phi}=0$ one can show (for completeness, the proof is given in \cref{lemma_weakmixingisback} in the appendix) that the set $A$ is weakly mixing in the sense that \[ \mathsf{d}^*\Big(\Big\{n:\big|\mathsf{d}_\Phi\big((A-n)\cap C\big)-\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)\mathsf{d}_\Phi(C)\big|>\varepsilon\Big\}\Big)=0 \] for any $\varepsilon>0$ and any set $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ for which all the implicit limits exist.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing U^2 seminorm gives weak mixing of A (Lemma 6.1).

nodes.name: Choose b_1
nodes.statement: Now choose $b_1\in A$ such that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi\big((A-b_1)\cap A\big)>0$. (Note that with respect to $\Phi$ a full-density set of $b_1\in A$ satisfies this.) Put $C_1:=A\cap(A-b_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick b_1 with A∩(A-b_1) of positive density.

nodes.name: Recursive choice
nodes.statement: Recursively, for each $n=2,3,\dots$ choose $b_n\in C_{n-1}$ such that \[ \mathsf{d}_\Phi\big(C_{n-1}\cap(A-b_n)\big)>0 \] and set $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap(A-b_n)$. It is clear that $B:=\{b_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subset A$ and that $B\oplus B\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose b_n ∈ C_{n-1} recursively; then B ⊂ A and B⊕B ⊂ A.

nodes.name: Reduce to k=2
nodes.statement: We prove this claim for the case $k=2$ and leave the general case to the interested reader.
nodes.statement_short: Treat only k = 2.

nodes.name: Containment from Proposition 3.27
nodes.statement: The fact that \[ A=\Bigl\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \{n^2\alpha\}\in \bigl[\tfrac{1}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\bigr]\Bigr\} \] contains $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}$ follows from \cref{prop_U2_implies_no_shift_needed}. In fact, since at each stage of the inductive construction in the proof of \cref{prop_U2_implies_no_shift_needed} there is a positive density set from which the members of $B$ can be drawn, there are in a sense many sets $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ for which $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: B ∪ B⊕B ⊂ A by Proposition 3.27.

nodes.name: Setup non-containment
nodes.statement: We are left with showing that $A$ does not contain $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\cup B^{\oplus 3}$. Let $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ be infinite.
nodes.statement_short: Show A contains no B ∪ B^{⊕2} ∪ B^{⊕3}; fix infinite B.

nodes.name: Ramsey refinement
nodes.statement: In view of Ramsey's theorem, replacing $B$ by an infinite subset of itself if needed, we can assume that for every distinct $b,b'\in B$, $\{bb'\alpha\}\approx_\varepsilon \gamma$ for some fixed $\gamma\in[0,1)$, where by $x \approx_\varepsilon y$ we mean that $|x-y| < C\varepsilon$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$. By further refining $B$ we can assume that $\{b^2\alpha\} \approx_\varepsilon \beta$ for every $b\in B$ and some $\beta\in[0,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Refine B so {bb'α} ≈ γ and {b^2α} ≈ β.

nodes.name: Expand squares
nodes.statement: If $B\subset A$ it follows that $\beta\approx_\varepsilon1/2$. If $B\oplus B\subset A$, expanding the square $(b+b')^2\alpha$ it follows that $2(\beta+\gamma)\approx_\varepsilon1/2$. If $B^{\oplus3}\subset A$, then expanding the square $(b_1+b_2+b_3)^2\alpha$ it follows that $3\beta+6\gamma\approx_\varepsilon1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Containments force β, 2β+2γ, 3β+6γ ≈ 1/2.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Since it is impossible that $\beta$, $2\beta+2\gamma$, and $3\beta+6\gamma$ are simultaneously close to $1/2$ modulo~$1$, it follows that $A$ cannot contain $B\cup B^{\oplus 2}\cup B^{\oplus 3}$.
nodes.statement_short: These three cannot all be near 1/2 mod 1.

nodes.name: Apply MRR
nodes.statement: Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)> 0$. By combining the results in~\cite[Section~2]{MRR}, we can find $\varepsilon > 0$, a F\o lner sequence $\Phi = (\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$, and a set $L\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that for every nonempty finite set $F\subset L$, the set $$ \bigcap_{x\in F}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr)> \varepsilon\Big\} $$ has positive density with respect to $\Phi$.
nodes.statement_short: From MRR get ε, Φ and L with positive-density intersections.

nodes.name: Define Q_i
nodes.statement: Let $F_1\subset F_2\subset \cdots\subset L$ be an exhaustion of $L$ by finite sets. For $i\in\mathbb{N}$, define \begin{equation} Q_i = \bigcap_{x\in F_i}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon\Big\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exhaust L by F_i and define Q_i.

nodes.name: Choose intervals J_i
nodes.statement: Pick $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for any interval $J\subset\mathbb{N}$ of length at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)$ and any set $E\subset J$ with $|E|\geq \delta |J|$, there exists $X\in\mathcal{D}$ with $X\subset E$. Set $\delta_i = \mathsf{d}_\Phi(Q_i)/2$ and for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, let $J_i\subset \mathbb{N}$ denote an interval whose length is at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$ and satisfies $$|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|. $$ Without loss of generality, we can further assume that for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\max J_i < \min J_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose long disjoint intervals J_i dense in Q_i.

nodes.name: Properties (i)-(ii)
nodes.statement: Then by~\eqref{eq:def-Qi}, it follows that \begin{enumerate} \item $F_i+(Q_i\cap J_i)\subset A$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$. \item If $n_1< n_2< \cdots$ is an enumeration of $\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}(J_i\cap Q_i)$, then $$\mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Derive properties (i) and (ii) from (14).

nodes.name: Property (i)
nodes.statement: $F_i+(Q_i\cap J_i)\subset A$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: F_i + (Q_i ∩ J_i) ⊂ A.

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: If $n_1< n_2< \cdots$ is an enumeration of $\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}(J_i\cap Q_i)$, then $$\mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon.$$
nodes.statement_short: Each n_k has d_Φ((A-n_k)∩L) > ε.

nodes.name: Intersectivity lemma
nodes.statement: Applying Bergelson's Intersectivity Lemma~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{bergelson}, there exists $K\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ such that for all nonempty finite sets $H\subset K$, we have \begin{equation} \mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{k\in H}\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bergelson's lemma yields K of density ε with positive-density intersections (15).

nodes.name: Choose X_i
nodes.statement: Define \[ R_i = \{n_k\colon k\in K\}\cap J_i\cap Q_i \] and let $I\subset\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set such that for all $i\in I$, we have \[ |R_i|\geq \frac{\varepsilon\delta_i}{2}|J_i| \] which exists because $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ and $|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|$. Since the length of $J_i$ exceeds $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$, we can find $X_i\in \mathcal{D}$ with $X_i\subset R_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Define R_i, an infinite index set I, and X_i ∈ D inside R_i.

nodes.name: Properties (iii)-(iv)
nodes.statement: Then by property~\ref{item:one} and~\eqref{eq:berg-cor}, we conclude that \begin{enumerate}[resume] \item $F_i+X_i\subset A$ for all $i\in I$. \item For each $i\in I$, we have $$\mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{x\in X_1\cup\ldots\cup X_i}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0. $$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Derive properties (iii) and (iv).

nodes.name: Property (iii)
nodes.statement: $F_i+X_i\subset A$ for all $i\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: F_i + X_i ⊂ A.

nodes.name: Property (iv)
nodes.statement: For each $i\in I$, we have $$\mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{x\in X_1\cup\ldots\cup X_i}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: Intersections over X_1 ∪ … ∪ X_i have positive density.

nodes.name: Base of construction
nodes.statement: We are now ready to inductively construct the sets $B_1, B_2,\ldots$ and $C_1, C_2, \ldots$. First choose $B_1\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $B_1\subset L$. Choose $i_1\in I$ sufficiently large such that $B_1\subset F_{i_1}$, and define $C_1 = X_{i_1}$. By Property~\eqref{item:three}, we have that $$B_1+C_1\subset A.$$
nodes.statement_short: Choose B_1 ⊂ L and C_1 = X_{i_1}.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assume we have defined the sets $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ and $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ such that $B_1, \ldots, B_n\subset L$ and $C_1 = X_{i_1}, \ldots, C_n = X_{i_n}$ for some $i_1 < i_2 < \ldots < i_n\in I$. Then by Property~\eqref{item:four}, there exists $B_{n+1}\in\mathcal{D}$ such that \[ B_{n+1}\subset\bigcap_{x\in X_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{i_n}}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr). \] It follows that $B_{n+1}\subset L$ and for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we have \[ B_{n+1}+C_k\subset A. \] Choose $i_{n+1}\in I$ that is sufficiently large such that \[ B_1\cup \cdots \cup B_n\cup B_{n+1}\subset F_{i_{n+1}} \] and set $C_{n+1} = X_{i_{n+1}}$. Then it follows from Property~\eqref{item:three} that for all $1 \leq k \leq n+1$, we have $$B_k+C_{n+1}\subset A, $$ completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Use (iv) to choose B_{n+1}, then (iii) to choose C_{n+1}.

nodes.name: Furstenberg correspondence
nodes.statement: Fix $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)>0$. By the Furstenberg correspondence principle (see~\cite{Furstenberg-book}), there exist a measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ and a set $E\in\mathcal{B}$ such that $\mu(E)=\mathsf{d}^*(A)$ and \begin{equation} \mathsf{d}^*((A-n_1)\cap\ldots\cap (A-n_j))\geq \mu(T^{-n_1}E\cap\ldots\cap T^{-n_j}E) \end{equation} for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n_1,\ldots,n_j\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer A to a system (X,B,μ,T) with set E satisfying (16).

nodes.name: Intersectivity
nodes.statement: Since $R$ is a set of strong recurrence, the sequence of sets $E_n=E\cap T^{-n}E$ satisfies $\limsup_{n\in R}\mu(E_n)>0$. Applying Bergelson's intersectivity lemma~\cite[Corollary~2.4]{bergelson} to the collection $\{E_n:n\in R\}$, there exists an infinite subset $L\subset R$ such that for any finite nonempty set $F\subset L$, the intersection $\bigcap_{n\in F} E_n$ has positive measure.
nodes.statement_short: Strong recurrence plus Bergelson's lemma give L ⊂ R with positive-measure intersections.

nodes.name: Back to A
nodes.statement: Combining this with~\eqref{eqn_furstenberg_correspondence_inequ}, we conclude that for any finite nonempty set $F\subset L$, the intersection \[ A\cap\biggl(\bigcap_{n\in F} (A-n)\biggr) \] has positive upper Banach density.
nodes.statement_short: By (16), A ∩ ⋂(A-n) has positive density for finite F ⊂ L.

nodes.name: Alternating construction
nodes.statement: In particular, this intersection is infinite and we use it to inductively construct the sets $B$ and $C$. Namely, let $\ell_1<\ell_2<\ldots$ be an enumeration of $L$ and choose $b_1:=\ell_1$ and then choose $c_1$ to be any element in the intersection $A\cap (A-b_1)$ with $c_1>b_1$. Let $b_2\in L$ be any element larger than $c_1$ and then choose $c_2$ to be any element in $A\cap (A-b_1)\cap (A-b_2)$ with $c_2>b_2$. Choose $b_3\in L$ larger than $c_2$ and take $c_3$ to be any element in the intersection $A\cap (A-b_1)\cap (A-b_2) \cap (A-b_3)$ with $c_3>b_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose b_i ∈ L and c_i ∈ A ∩ ⋂(A-b_j) alternately.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Continuing this procedure, we obtain sets $C\subset A$ and $B\subset R$ with $\{b+c: b\in B,~c\in C,~b<c\}\subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: The construction yields B ⊂ R, C ⊂ A as required.

nodes.name: Assume for contradiction
nodes.statement: Suppose, for the sake of a contradiction, that $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfy~\eqref{eq_primestraus}. Then $p_n:=x_n-t$ is prime for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume (17); then p_n = x_n - t are primes.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole indices
nodes.statement: Find a set of indices $F\subset\mathbb{N}$ with size $|F|=p_1$ and $\min F>1$, such that every prime $p_i$ with $i\in F$ has the same congruence class $\bmod\,p_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick p_1 primes in one residue class mod p_1.

nodes.name: Form q
nodes.statement: Then on the one hand $$q:=(p_1+t)+\sum_{i\in F}(p_i+t)\in\mathbb{P}+t$$ by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Their sum with p_1 + t lies in P + t.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: On the other hand, $q\equiv t\bmod p_1$, so $q-t$ is both a prime and a multiple of $p_1$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: q - t is a prime multiple of p_1, contradiction.

nodes.name: Probability of an interval
nodes.statement: More precisely, if $(p_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a decreasing sequence and for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}p_n\cdot n^{\varepsilon}\to\infty \] then for every $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, the probability that the interval $[n+1,n+k]$ is contained in $A$ is $\prod_{i=1}^kp_{n+i}$, which is approximately equal to $p_n^k$.
nodes.statement_short: The interval [n+1,n+k] lies in A with probability ≈ p_n^k.

nodes.name: Borel-Cantelli
nodes.statement: Since for disjoint intervals these events are independent and eventually have probability larger than $1/n$, by the second Borel-Cantelli lemma it follows that $A$ contains infinitely many intervals of length $k$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Second Borel-Cantelli gives infinitely many such intervals.

nodes.name: A is thick
nodes.statement: Since this holds for every $k$, the set $A$ is thick (see \cref{def:thick_synd_ps}) almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Hence A is thick almost surely.

nodes.name: Choose N_j
nodes.statement: For each $j\in\mathbb{N}$, using the F\o lner property, we choose the smallest $N_j$ such that for any $N>N_j$, the first $j$ columns of $\Phi_N$ account for less than $1/j$ of the total cardinality of $\Phi_N$. More precisely, if $N> N_j$, then \begin{equation*} \sum_{n>j}\big|(\Phi_N)_n\big|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose N_j so the first j columns are a 1/j fraction of Φ_N for N > N_j.

nodes.name: Define the columns
nodes.statement: Let $M_j=\max\{m:(j,m)\in\Phi_N,N\leq N_j\}=\max\bigcup_{N\leq N_j}(\Phi_N)_j$ and take $A$ to be the set described in terms of its columns by $A_j=\{1,\dots,M_j\}$. Note that if $n\geq j$ and $N\leq N_j$, then $A_j\supset(\Phi_N)_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Let column j of A be {1,…,M_j}.

nodes.name: Density one
nodes.statement: It follows that for $N\in[N_j,N_{j+1}]$, $$|A\cap\Phi_N|=\sum_n|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|\geq\sum_{n>j}|A_n\cap(\Phi_N)_n|=\sum_{n>j}|(\Phi_N)_n|\geq|\Phi_N|(1-1/j),$$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A)=1$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Counting columns n > j gives d_Φ(A) = 1.

nodes.name: Dense fibers
nodes.statement: By assumption on the set $A$, there are $a > 0$ and $n(1)<n(2)<\ldots\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_{n(i)}) \ge a$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find fibers A_{n(i)} of density ≥ a.

nodes.name: Intersectivity
nodes.statement: It follows from~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{bergelson} that, after possibly passing to a sub-F\o{}lner{} sequence, there is a subsequence $r(1), r(2), \ldots$ of the sequence $n(1),n(2),\ldots$ with \[ \mathsf{d}_\Phi(A_{r(1)} \cap A_{r(2)} \cap \cdots \cap A_{r(i)}) > 0 \] for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bergelson's lemma gives a subsequence with positive-density finite intersections.

nodes.name: Choose b(i), c(i)
nodes.statement: Inductively choose $b(i)$ and $c(i)$ with $c(i) \in A_{b(1)} \cap \cdots \cap A_{b(i)}$ and $b(i+1) > c(i) > b(i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose b(i), c(i) alternately inside the intersections.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Taking $B = \{b(i) : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $C = \{ c(i) : i \in \mathbb{N} \}$, the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: B and C as constructed work.

nodes.name: Van der Corput
nodes.statement: First estimate \begin{align*} & \left| \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n)g(j) \right|^2 \\ \le &{} \limsup_{M \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n+m) g(j+m) f(j+n) g(j) \right| \end{align*} using the van der Corput inequality.
nodes.section: 6 Uniformity norms and weak mixing functions
nodes.statement_short: Bound the squared correlation by van der Corput.

nodes.name: Drop absolute values
nodes.statement: The limit as $M \to \infty$ of the quantity inside $| \cdot |$ is non-negative, and so we may dispense in the limit with the absolute values.
nodes.section: 6 Uniformity norms and weak mixing functions
nodes.statement_short: The limit is non-negative, so absolute values can be dropped.

nodes.name: Cesàro average and Hölder
nodes.statement: Then taking the Ces\`{a}ro{} average in $N$, we obtain \begin{align*} & \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \left| \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n) g(j) \right|^2 \\ \le & \lim_{N \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \lim_{M \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \lim_{J \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{|\Phi_J|} \sum_{j \in \Phi_J} f(j+n+m) g(j+m) f(j+n) g(j) \end{align*} and H\"{o}lder{}'s inequality shows that this last term is zero whenever $\ghkn{f}_\un{2}{\Phi}$ equals zero.
nodes.section: 6 Uniformity norms and weak mixing functions
nodes.statement_short: Average in N and apply Hölder; the U^2 seminorm vanishes.

nodes.name: WLOG 0 in H
nodes.statement: By shifting $H$ we may assume without loss of generality that $0\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift H so that 0 ∈ H.

nodes.name: Define N and Q
nodes.statement: Let $N=|H|+\sum_{p|q}p$, where the sum runs over all prime divisors of $q$. Let $\tilde Q=\prod_{p\leq N}p$ where the product is taken over all primes smaller than $N$, use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to find $L$ such that $L\equiv (\tilde Q/p)^{-1}\bmod p$ for every prime $p<N$ and let $Q=\tilde QL$. Note that $Q/p\equiv1\bmod p$ for every prime $p<N$.
nodes.statement_short: Define N, Q̃, L and Q with Q/p ≡ 1 mod p.

nodes.name: Define enlarged set
nodes.statement: For each prime divisor $p$ of $q$, let $H_p=\big\{x\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}:x+a\not\equiv0\bmod p\big\}$, and let $$\tilde H=H\cup\bigcup_{p|q}\frac Qp\cdot H_p.$$
nodes.statement_short: Enlarge H by multiples of Q/p blocking residues.

nodes.name: Claim and reduction
nodes.statement: We claim that $\tilde H$ is admissible. Assuming the claim for now, notice that if $n+\tilde H\subset\mathbb{P}$, then $n+H\subset\mathbb{P}$. Moreover, if $n\not\equiv a\bmod q$, then for some prime $p|q$ we have $n\not\equiv a\bmod p$, and hence there is some $x\in H_p$ with $x+n\equiv0\bmod p$. Therefore $h:=x\tfrac Q p\in \tilde H$ and satisfies $h+n\equiv0\bmod p$ which implies that $h+n$ is not a prime (unless $n<q$). From \cref{conj_hardylittlewood}, we conclude that there exist infinitely many $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ and $n\equiv a\bmod q$.
nodes.statement_short: Assuming H̃ admissible, DHL for H̃ forces n ≡ a mod q.

nodes.name: Primes for H
nodes.statement: Assuming the claim for now, notice that if $n+\tilde H\subset\mathbb{P}$, then $n+H\subset\mathbb{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: n + H̃ ⊂ P gives n + H ⊂ P.

nodes.name: Wrong residues excluded
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $n\not\equiv a\bmod q$, then for some prime $p|q$ we have $n\not\equiv a\bmod p$, and hence there is some $x\in H_p$ with $x+n\equiv0\bmod p$. Therefore $h:=x\tfrac Q p\in \tilde H$ and satisfies $h+n\equiv0\bmod p$ which implies that $h+n$ is not a prime (unless $n<q$).
nodes.statement_short: If n ≢ a mod q some element of n + H̃ is divisible by p.

nodes.name: Apply DHL
nodes.statement: From \cref{conj_hardylittlewood}, we conclude that there exist infinitely many $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ and $n\equiv a\bmod q$.
nodes.statement_short: DHL for H̃ yields infinitely many good n.

nodes.name: Remains: admissibility
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $\tilde H$ is admissible.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the claim.

nodes.name: Large primes
nodes.statement: Note that \[ |\tilde{H}| \le |H| + \sum_{p|q} |H_p| \le |H| + \sum_{p|q} p = N \] so for every prime $p>N$ we trivially have less than $p$ residue classes mod $p$ represented in $\tilde H$.
nodes.statement_short: |H̃| ≤ N, so primes p > N are fine.

nodes.name: Primes not dividing q
nodes.statement: For each $p<N$, if $p$ does not divide $q$ then any $h\in\tilde H\setminus H$ is a multiple of $p$; since $0\in H$ and $H$ is admissible we conclude that there are less than $p$ residue classes mod $p$ represented in $\tilde H$.
nodes.statement_short: For p < N, p ∤ q, added elements are multiples of p.

nodes.name: Primes dividing q
nodes.statement: Finally, if $p|q$, then for any $p'\neq p$, each element of $\tfrac Q{p'}\cdot H_{p'}$ is a multiple of $p$. Since no element of $H$ is congruent to $-a\bmod p$, no element of $H_p$ is congruent to $-a\bmod p$ and $\tfrac Qp\equiv1\bmod p$, we conclude that no element of $\tilde H$ is congruent to $-a\bmod p$.
nodes.statement_short: For p | q, the residue -a mod p is missed.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: Given $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$ denote by $[n]:=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ and denote by $[n]^{<k}:=\{F\subset[n]:|F|<k\}$. We stress that $[n]^{<k}$ includes the empty set.
nodes.statement_short: Define [n] and [n]^{<k}.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Our goal (cf.\ \cref{conjecture_primestrueHindman}) is to construct, for a given fixed $k\in\mathbb{N}$, a strictly increasing sequence $b:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{equation} \forall n\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall F\in[n]^{<k+1},\ F\neq\varnothing, \qquad \sum_{i\in F}b(i)\in\mathbb{P}-1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Construct b with all nonempty ≤k-fold sums in P-1 (24).

nodes.name: Auxiliary residues
nodes.statement: We construct additionally, for each prime $p$, some $x_p\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ such that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in\mathbb{P}$, \begin{equation} p<k2^{n}\ \Rightarrow\ b(n)\equiv x_p\bmod p \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \forall F\in[n]^{<k},\ \forall\ell\leq k-|F|,\qquad p\not|\left(1+\ell x_p+\sum_{i\in F}b(i)\right) \end{equation} both hold.
nodes.statement_short: Also construct residues x_p satisfying (25) and (26).

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Let $b(1)\in\mathbb{P}-1$ be divisible by each prime $p< 2k$, and set $x_p:=0$ for those primes. That such a $b(1)$ exists follows from Dirichlet's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Choose b(1) ∈ P-1 divisible by all p < 2k (Dirichlet).

nodes.name: Inductive step: choose x_p
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $m>1$ and we have chosen $b(1),\dots,b(m-1)$ and $(x_p)_{p<k2^{m-1}}$ satisfying~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimesb}, \eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} and~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} for all $n<m$ and each prime $p<k2^{m-1}$. For each prime $p\in(k2^{m-1},k2^{m})$ choose an arbitrary $x_p$ such that \begin{equation} \forall F\in[m-1]^{<k},\ \forall\ell\leq k,\qquad p\not|\left(1+\ell x_p+\sum_{i\in F}b(i)\right). \end{equation} Note that there are at most $k2^{m-1}$ values of $x_p\bmod p$ that do \emph{not} satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}; therefore for each $p>k2^{m-1}$ we can choose a value of $x_p$ that does satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}. Observe that this choice of $x_p$ satisfies~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} for all $n<m$ and $p<k2^{m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose new residues x_p avoiding (27) for primes in (k2^{m-1}, k2^m).

nodes.name: Define a and H
nodes.statement: Let $q=\prod_{p<k2^{m}}p$ and use the Chinese remainder theorem to find $a\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a\equiv x_p\bmod p$ for every $p<k2^{m}$. Next let $$H:=\left\{1+\sum_{i\in F}b(i):F\in[m-1]^{<k}\right\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: CRT gives a; H collects 1 + earlier partial sums.

nodes.name: H admissible
nodes.statement: Note that $|H|\leq 2^{m-1}$. It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} that for each $p<2^{m-1}\leq k2^{m-1}$, $|\{b(n)\bmod p:n\leq m-1\}|\leq1+\log_2(p/k)< p$ and hence that $H$ is an admissible set. It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} that $(a+h,q)=1$ for every $h\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: H is admissible and (a+h, q) = 1 by (25), (26).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 7.4
nodes.statement: In view of \cref{lemma_DHLinprogressions}, there exists $b(m)>b(m-1)$ such that $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ and $b(m)\equiv a\bmod q$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 7.4 gives b(m) with b(m)+H ⊂ P and b(m) ≡ a mod q.

nodes.name: Verify induction
nodes.statement: From $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimesb} holds with $n=m$. From $b(m)\equiv a\bmod q$ and the fact that $a\equiv x_p\bmod p$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} holds with $n=m$. Finally, from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} holds with $n=m$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check (24)-(26) hold for n = m.
